transcript:
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
Junior military leaders are expected to hear today about more cuts among the top brass
when Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth addresses them today.
NPR's Quill Lawrence reports Hegseth has reshaped the senior ranks of the force.
Last year, Hegseth commanded senior leaders from all over the world to attend a speech
where he mostly talked about themes from his book, The War on Warriors.
This year, it will be junior officers and enlisted leaders in the audience, handpicked
in part for their physical appearance.
Hegseth is expected to announce a 20 percent cut of admirals and generals' posts on top
of the purge he's already conducted of senior officers, many of them black or female.
Hegseth has often cited cultural issues and says he's restoring a warrior ethos to the
military.
Critics in Congress say Hegseth should be consulting with lawmakers and offering explanations for
firing highly experienced and widely respected military leaders while the country is at war.
Quill Lawrence, NPR News.
And according to a memo from Hegseth yesterday, the Defense Department will also no longer
appoint civilians as tenured college faculty at the U.S.'s Military Service Academies.
Well, 23 years after the U.S. invasion of Iraq, American forces are officially out,
NPR's Jana Raft says this is not the first time the U.S. has withdrawn.
In 2011, after a disagreement with Iraq over the status of U.S. forces here, they left.
And then they were invited back by Iraq three years later to fight ISIS.
So they've stayed since then as part of the U.S.-led international coalition that has
been fighting the militant group.
NPR's Jana Raft reporting, NPR has learned of a plan for a massive new data center on
federal land in Utah.
NPR's Jeff Bromfield reports it would involve building hundreds of nuclear reactors.
The proposal seen by NPR came from the company Valor Atomics.
Valor already has a test reactor operating in Utah, but it wants to build around 450
more small nuclear reactors on 9,000 acres of federal land.
The reactors would provide power for data centers, among other things.
Neil Clark with the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance says Valor isn't the only company
quietly seeking to build data centers on public lands.
It's pretty obvious that they are trying to keep these proposals and these processes
totally under the radar to make sure the public is kept in the dark.
The Bureau of Land Management says the public will have an opportunity to comment on the
proposal after the agency reviews the application for completeness.
Jeff Bromfield, NPR News.
Federal judges ruled that the Trump administration can deport the Palestinian-born leader of
Wisconsin's largest mosque.
The government said Salah Sarsour poses a foreign policy threat.
It cites terrorism convictions in Israel from decades ago.
The administration also accuses Sarsour of lying about it when he applied for a green
carpet.
The judge rejected that argument.
You're listening to NPR News.
The United Kingdom is advising all of its universities to cut ties with the China General
Technology Research Institute.
The government accuses the Chinese government of using the facility to develop spy technology.
Britain's domestic intelligence agency, MI5, says more than 100 academics tied to the UK
have worked on projects secretly funded by Chinese intelligence.
The U.S. economies expanded at a pace of 2.2 percent in the second quarter, the Commerce
Department saying consumer spending and business investment were strong.
Consumer spending accounts for about 70 percent of U.S. economic activity.
Backpack is getting a lot of social media adoration after emerging the chunky champion
of Alaska's Fat Bear Week with an estimated weight of more than 1,000 pounds.
Alaska Public Media's Ava White has more.
Backpack, also known as number 89, got his nickname because he'd hold onto his mama's
back as they'd cross the Brooks River in Katmai National Park and Preserve.
He's now 20 years old.
Backpack has gained so much weight over the summer that his before and after photos look
like totally different brown bears.
Katmai park ranger Sarah Bruce says Backpack isn't an aggressive bear.
He's more of like a stoic presence on the river.
He doesn't really get into drama or cause any upset in the hierarchy.
He holds his own very quietly.
His victory was declared Tuesday evening after he triumphed in the competition that drew a
record number of voters from around the world.
For NPR News, I'm Ava White in Anchorage.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to announce 20 percent cut of admirals and generals' posts
Pentagon will no longer appoint civilians as tenured faculty at Military Service Academies
American forces officially withdraw from Iraq after 23 years since initial U.S. invasion
Company Valor Atomics proposes massive data center with 450 small nuclear reactors on Utah federal land
Federal judges rule Trump administration can deport Palestinian-born leader of Wisconsin's largest mosque
United Kingdom advises universities to cut ties with China General Technology Research Institute
U.S. economy expanded at 2.2 percent pace in second quarter, Commerce Department reports
Bear named Backpack wins Alaska's Fat Bear Week competition at Katmai National Park
